title: 1984 Balkan Bulgarian Tupolev Tu-134 crash
summary: A Balkan Bulgarian Airlines Tupolev Tu-134 crashed while on approach to Sofia Airport in heavy snow, killing all 50 aboard. The crew failed to make visual contact with the ground as they descended below decision altitude. The aircraft hit a power line and crashed 4 kilometers from the runway into a forest.

factors.evidence: while on approach in heavy snow
crew descended below decision altitude without visual contact
aircraft crashed 4 km from runway into forest

events.text: Crew descended below decision altitude while on approach to Sofia in heavy snow
Aircraft struck power line during low-altitude descent
Aircraft crashed into forest 4 km from runway, destroying the aircraft with no survivors

notes: Text provides minimal investigation details; only basic facts of accident are stated

title: 1984 Biman Bangladesh Airlines Fokker F27 crash
summary: In poor weather with heavy rain and very low visibility, the crew attempted a VOR approach to runway 32 but missed the runway and executed a missed approach. A second missed approach was executed on an ILS approach to runway 14 as both pilots failed to spot the runway. On the third approach, the aircraft descended too low while still several hundred meters from the runway, but neither crew member realized this due to poor visibility, and the aircraft crashed into a swamp about 550 meters short of the runway.
probable_cause: The crew's failure to maintain situational awareness during approach in poor visibility resulted in descent below safe altitude without required visual references, causing controlled flight into terrain short of the runway.

factors.evidence: weather conditions in Dhaka were poor; turbulence and heavy rain made visibility very poor
the plane got too low while it was still several hundred meters from the runway
as the runway was not spotted by either crew member, a missed approach was executed
neither crew member realized this due to the poor visibility
the plane crashed into a swamp about 550 meters short of the runway

events.text: Crew first attempted VOR approach to runway 32 in poor weather with turbulence and heavy rain
Runway was not spotted by either crew member, missed approach was executed
Crew tried ILS approach on runway 14 but missed approach executed again as both pilots failed to spot runway
On third approach plane got too low several hundred meters from runway but crew did not realize due to poor visibility and crashed into swamp 550 meters short of runway

title: 1984 San Luis Obispo mid-air collision

aircraft.type: Beechcraft C-99 Commuter and Rockwell Commander 112

summary: Wings West Airlines Flight 628, a Beechcraft C-99 climbing after departure, collided head-on at 3400 ft with Rockwell Commander 112 returning to San Luis Obispo on instrument training flight without flight plan. All 17 on both aircraft perished. NTSB determined both pilots elected to fly VFR rather than IFR, preventing ATC from detecting collision threat.
probable_cause: Decisions of pilots of both aircraft to fly under visual flight rules; had they flown IFR, air traffic control would have been warned of imminent collision and could have instructed evasive action.

factors.evidence: pilots of Flight 628 failed to monitor local aviation radio transmissions, monitoring appropriate frequency for only first 5 miles
both aircraft chose to fly VFR instead of IFR despite being in controlled airspace
because neither aircraft was flying IFR, air traffic controllers were not closely monitoring aircraft flight paths
despite clear skies Beechcraft pilots would have noticed Commander only 10 seconds before collision while Commander pilots saw Beechcraft 6-8 seconds before
Flight 628 collided head-on with Commander at altitude 3400 ft

events.text: Wings West Flight 628 left gate at San Luis Obispo-County Airport at 11:10 am, took off from runway 29 six minutes later bound for San Francisco
Flight 628 cleared for San Francisco and to climb and maintain altitude 7000 ft
Meanwhile Rockwell Commander had taken off from same airport at 10:55 am without flight plan and was returning for approach
Flight 628 collided head-on with Commander at 3400 ft; both aircraft destroyed

notes: Clear weather and daylight made collision surprising but visual detection inadequate
VFR-vs-IFR decision was central factor identified by NTSB

title: Aeroflot 3352
summary: A Tupolev Tu-154 descending to land at Omsk struck maintenance vehicles on the runway, killing all 178 people on board. The ground controller fell asleep on duty, failed to engage the runway-occupied warning, and incorrectly authorized runway maintenance. Poorly lit maintenance vehicles were invisible to the approaching pilots.
probable_cause: The aircraft struck maintenance vehicles on the runway due to the controller falling asleep, failing to implement required safety procedures, and inadequate vehicle lighting.

factors.evidence: The 23-year-old ground controller was inexperienced and had insufficient sleep in days before the accident.
Ground controller fell asleep and did not switch on the runway occupied warning.
Maintenance crew kept vehicle lights on only at start and finish, preventing pilots from seeing vehicles on runway.
Flight was approaching in poor weather with light rain and 3 km visibility with 100 m ceiling.
Aircraft struck three maintenance vehicles positioned on the runway at 5:36 a.m.

events.text: Maintenance crew requested permission to dry runway; ground controller gave permission then fell asleep and forgot to activate runway occupied warning.
Three maintenance vehicles moved to runway: UAZ-469 with trailer followed by KrAZ and Ural trucks.
Maintenance crew attempted to contact ground control three times about runway lights but received no response.
Flight 3352 requested permission to land; aircraft struck maintenance vehicles on runway at high speed.

notes: deadliest aviation accident on Russian territory at time
ground controller sentenced to 15 years, died by suicide in prison

title: PBA 1039
summary: PBA Flight 1039 received takeoff clearance and began the takeoff roll from Runway 31. Thirty seconds after takeoff, witnesses saw the aircraft in a steep descent. The horizontal stabilizer, elevators, tail cone, and ventral fin separated from the aircraft in flight. Investigation found fractures in hinge brackets from overstress and multiple potential causes including elevator control system or trim system malfunction.
probable_cause: Structural failure of elevator control system or elevator trim system that resulted in an overstressed elevator control rod, ultimately leading to separation of elevators and horizontal stabilizer.

factors.evidence: horizontal stabilizer separated with elevators due to fractures in hinge brackets typical of overstress separations
the aircraft design lacked fail-safe elevator control systems susceptible to overstress separation
the lack of cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder hampered investigation
horizontal stabilizer and elevators separated from aircraft in flight
the structural failure resulted in loss of control and aircraft crashed
the EMB 110 crashed approximately 7800 feet beyond the end of Runway 31

events.text: At 6:12 p.m., Flight 1039 received takeoff clearance and began its takeoff roll down Runway 31.
The EMB 110 climbed above the departure end of Runway 31 and was told to switch to departure control frequency.
Thirty seconds after takeoff, witnesses saw the aircraft in a steep descent.
The horizontal stabilizer, elevators, tail cone assembly, and part of the ventral fin separated from the aircraft while in flight.
The EMB 110 crashed approximately 7800 feet beyond the end of Runway 31 and was destroyed by the impact and a post-crash fire.

title: Aeroflot 3519
summary: Two minutes after takeoff at 2,040 meters, the No. 3 engine failed due to a metallurgical defect in the compressor disk and caught fire. The flight engineer mistakenly shut down the No. 2 engine instead of the failed No. 3 engine. The fire spread to the pylon and auxiliary power unit, destroying the electrical and hydraulic systems. The aircraft crashed into the runway at a 50-degree angle. One passenger survived with severe injuries.
probable_cause: Engine failure due to metallurgical defect in first stage low pressure compressor disk, compounded by the flight engineer shutting down the wrong engine, and subsequent fire spread through the aircraft.

factors.evidence: Two minutes and one second into the flight, at a speed of 480 km/h and an altitude of 2040 m, the No. 3 (starboard) engine failed and caught fire. This was due to a metallurgical and manufacturing defect in the first stage low pressure compressor disk.
The flight engineer mistakenly shut down the No. 2 (center) engine; ten seconds later, he realized his error and attempted to restart it.
By that time, the fire from the No. 3 engine had spread to the pylon and the auxiliary power unit in the rear compartment and continued to spread to the No. 2 engine.
The fire damaged the aircraft's electrical system, causing the voltage to drop and the hydraulics to fail.
Due to the extensive fire damage that left the aircraft with only one functional engine, the crew was unable to control the plane.
the fire from the No. 3 engine had spread to the pylon and the auxiliary power unit

events.text: Two minutes and one second into the flight, at a speed of 480 km/h and an altitude of 2040 m, the No. 3 (starboard) engine failed and caught fire.
The flight engineer mistakenly shut down the No. 2 (center) engine.
Ten seconds later, he realized his error and attempted to restart it.
The fire from the No. 3 engine had spread to the pylon and the auxiliary power unit in the rear compartment and continued to spread to the No. 2 engine.
The fire damaged the aircraft's electrical system, causing the voltage to drop and the hydraulics to fail.
It banked to the right and crashed into the runway at 2:15 pm at a 50-degree angle.
